query: How will we implement and report staggered-DiD estimators (weighting, ATT vs. group effects) and which sensitivity checks will probe staggered-treatment assumptions?

response.query: How will we implement and report staggered-DiD estimators (weighting, ATT vs. group effects) and which sensitivity checks will probe staggered-treatment assumptions?
response.answer: Implement staggered-DiD using two-way fixed effects or local projections; report ATT and group effects; sensitivity checks include pre-trend tests and robustness to exclusion periods.

results.title: How Much Should We Trust Staggered Difference-In
results.content: In settings with more than two units and two time periods, the regression DiD model usually takes the following two-way ﬁxed eﬀect (TWFE) form: yit = αi + λt + δDDDit + ϵit, (2) where αi and λt are unit and time period ﬁxed eﬀects, which subsume the main eﬀects for Di and POSTt. Researchers commonly modify this TWFE model to include covariates, time trends, and dynamic treatment eﬀect estimation (e.g., by separately including indicators for the number of periods before or after the treatment).2 Notably, researchers apply the TWFE model to estimate δ in settings with staggered treatment timing. 3.1 Static Staggered DiD Estimates Goodman-Bacon (2021) shows that the “static” staggered DiD TWFE treatment eﬀect estimate (δDD of Eq., (2)) is a “weighted average of all possible two-group/two-period DiD estimators in the data.” For example, the TWFE estimate constitutes four possible 2x2s when there are three groups over the sample period (from from the earlierst period—t0—to the last period in the data—T): a never-treated group (denoted U), an earlier-treated group (denoted k) that is treated at time t∗ k, and a later-treated group (denoted l) that is treated at t∗ l .3 The ﬁrst two of the possible 2x2 DiD comparisons involve one treatment group (either the earlier- or the later-treated ﬁrms) and the untreated group (as control) over the whole sample window (from t0 to T). To the extent this occurs, these outcome trends are inappropriate counterfactuals for the later-treated units.4 Eq., (4) suggests the staggered DiD TWFE estimate can diﬀer from the sample-average ATT due to treatment eﬀect heterogeneity either over time or across groups, even when the parallel-trends assumption is satisﬁed (V WCT = 0). Sun and Abraham (2021) shows that the choice of exclusion periods could lead to biases in TWFE dynamic eﬀect estimates, particularly when researchers exclude post-treatment relative-time periods from event-study speciﬁcations. Simulation: TWFE Dynamic Treatment Eﬀect Estimates with No Real Pre-Trends and Actual Pre-Trends Figure 5, left-hand panel, plots the distribution of event-study estimates based on a variant of Simulation 6 (Eq., (10)) in which there are no pre-period trends and post-treatment trend-breaks of the three diﬀerent cohorts are δ1989 = 0.10σROA, δ1998 = 0.05σROA, and δ1998 = 0.01σROA, where σROA is the empirical ROA standard deviation in Compustat.

results.title: GitHub - danielegirardi/lpdid: Implementing Local Projections Difference-in-Differences (LP-DiD) estimators
results.content: LP-DiD uses local projections to estimate dynamic effects, while restricting the estimation sample to units entering treatment and 'clean' controls, thus avoiding the 'negative-weighting' bias of TWFE estimators. A baseline LP-DiD specification for staggered and absorbing treatment settings can be written as follows.1 Assume panel data for $N$ units (indexed by $i$) and $T$ periods (indexed by $t$). Under the usual DiD assumptions, OLS estimation of this baseline LP-DiD specification yields a variance-weighted average treatment effect on the treated (VWATT), giving more weight to more precisely estimated cohort-specific effects. LP-DiD can accommodate non-absorbing treatment, meaning that units can enter and exit treatment multiple times, through appropriate modification of the clean control condition. * **lpdid\_regression\_adjustment.do** focuses on the Regression Adjustment LP-DiD estimator with covariates (Dube, Girardi, Jorda' and Taylor 2023, Sec 4.1.1) and illustrates four alternative ways to implement it, using the STATA official commands 'teffects ra' or 'margins' or the user-written alternatives 'kmatch ra' or 'listreg'.

results.title: A Generalized Difference-in-Differences Estimator for Randomized Stepped-Wedge and Observational Staggered Adoption Settings
results.content: Across settings, the analysis of the data generated from staggered treatment adoption requires careful consideration of the desired estimand, assumptions about the treatment effect, consideration of heterogeneity across units, time periods, and treatment regimens, and appropriate consideration of variance and correlation. In the observational staggered adoption setting, approaches to address the biases that can arise in two-way fixed-effects models (see, e.g., Goodman-Bacon (2021) and Imai & Kim (2021)) have included adjusting the interpretation based on the identifying assumptions as in Athey & Imbens (2022), specifying “dynamic” (time-varying) treatment effects as in Sun & Abraham (2021), and isolating, excluding, or weighting effect estimators targeting specific group-time effects as in Callaway & Sant’Anna (2021) and de Chaisemartin & D’Haultfœuille (2020). The first group were designed for the staggered adoption setting- (see Arkhangelsky & Imbens (2024) for a summary), the second group specifically target the effect in the first period on treatment, and the last estimator uses only vertical comparisons.

results.title: DDD Estimators, Distributional Effects, Causal Diagrams, and Cross-Field Counterfactuals
results.content: This paper extends the Quantile Treatment Effect on the Treated (QTT) framework to multiple time periods and staggered adoption settings. Andrea proposes a method to estimate distributional treatment effects in settings with multiple periods, staggered adoption, and non-experimental data. Andrea uses a combination of distributional parallel trends and a copula invariance assumption to identify the full counterfactual distribution of untreated outcomes for the treated group. It also matters methodologically: while earlier papers offered theoretical identification of distributional effects under staggered DiD, Andrea is the first to provide a fully worked-out estimator. In summary, Andrea’s paper gives applied researchers a way to estimate how the entire outcome distribution would have evolved in the absence of treatment, even in complex staggered DiD settings. Instead of relying on visual pre-trend checks or hoping for the best, you can use a causal diagram to make your assumptions explicit and formally test whether PT is likely to hold.

results.title: Staggered DiD versus traditional DiD - What is different? | Welcome to my homepage!
results.content: ## Can we apply our traditional DiD strategy to realities with staggered treatment adoption? They investigate how estimators in this staggered setting can be interpreted, and find that they are weighted averages of causal effects and bias terms. One of these papers is the paper by Athey and Imbens (2018) which concludes that under random treatment assignment the standard Difference-In-Differences estimator is an unbiased estimator of a particular weighted average causal effect. To derive their results, Athey and Imbens (2018) consider a setting with i=1,…,N individuals and t=1,…,T time periods, with a binary treatment being first adopted in t=T+1. They then define a fraction of individuals belonging to each timing-treatment-group, and the population average of the potential outcome in period t for adoption date a:. and the average causal effect of adoption date a′ relative to a, on the outcome in period t as:. * Assumption 1: Random adoption date. Put differently, there is no causal effect of an early or late adoption of the treatment on the outcome of interest. Athey and Imbens (2018) give an example of this exclusion restriction, that is, when our cohorts differ per period (pooled panel data), as for example in the case that we estimate the effect of a student subsidy on the employment rate of 25-year olds. The first of these auxiliary assumptions is the assumption about constant treatment effects across units. The second auxiliary assumption states that treatment effects are constant over time. Athey and Imbens (2018) in a next step derive the difference-in-difference estimator in the staggered design, and analyze its interpretation. with \(\tau\) being our main variable of interest, assuming treatment effects to be additive and constant across time periods and units. They interprete the DiD estimand under the random adoption assumption, therefore leading to a different result than previous paper analyzing the estimate. They then show that the staggered DiD estimator is a weighted average of simple estimators for the causal effect of changes in the adoption dates, which they call \(\tau\_{t, aa'}\). Imposing the no-anticipation assumption, the last average has weights summing up to 1 instead of -1, and the interpretation of the overall DiD estimator is easier.
